newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed in pre-weekend U.S. activity.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed in pre-weekend U.S. activity.

text.p: The dollar ended marginally lower versus the yen but rose with the pound against the mark in the aftermath of a stunning victory by Britain's Labour Party in national elections, currency experts said.

Initially, the pound tumbled in Asia partly in reaction to an editorial in London's The Times newspaper that said the new government "must create conditions for (an) immediate fall in the pound" to avoid economic damage.
The newspaper article also said taxes need to rise in Britain to counter the pressure for higher interest rates.
Experts linked the pound's recovery to the fact that its sell-off was overdone and to position-squaring before a long weekend as Britons celebrate the Early May holiday on Monday.
The pound slid below 2.76 marks in Europe but it later rebounded more than four pfennigs in New York.
As the pound climbed against the mark, it helped pull the dollar higher versus the German currency.
Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International, said the pound's recovery against the mark "is supportive of dollar-mark but not overly so."
The pound traded near 2.8052/62 marks in late dealings, up from around 2.7790/00 in very early activity.
The dollar closed at 1.7290/00 marks, up from 1.7235/45 at the open. Against the yen, the dollar edged lower to 126.60/65 from 126.66/71.
Some experts pointed to gains in U.S. stocks and government securities as factors that supported the dollar.
The Dow industrial average finished up 94.72 points or 1.36 percent at 7071.20. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond closed 15/32 higher at 96.26/32 to yield 6.88 percent.
"Those are not reasons to go and sell the dollar," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc, referring to the gains in stocks and bonds.
A key report on employment conditions in the United States sent mixed signals to the currency market on Friday.
The Labor Department reported that the economy created 142,000 non-farm payroll jobs in April, a figure that was well below the 211,000 gain expected in a Reuters poll.
The amount of jobs added in March was revised down to 139,000 from a previously reported 175,000.
Furthermore, the length of the average work week shrank to 34.6 hours in April from 34.9 hours in March, while average hourly earnings fell one cent in April to $12.14.
In contrast to the other data, the jobless rate fell to 4.9 percent in April, its lowest since a 4.8 percent rate in November of 1973. The rate in March stood at 5.2 percent.
"They saw moderate numbers, that's why they sold the dollar as the initial reaction," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.
"But then they realized the unemployment rate was down to 4.9 percent...and they bought the dollar back," he added.
Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.4707/17 Swiss francs, up from 1.4685/95 francs at the open.
The pound rose to $1.6215/25 from $1.6108/18.
The dollar slid to Canadian $1.3805/10 from C$1.3841/46.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7826/31, down from $0.7838/43.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
